source_title: California real estate CEO sentenced to 18 months over $2.2m investor losses
source_excerpt: A real-estate business can face financial difficulties, but concealing those problems from investors can turn a struggling company into a fraud case. A California property developer who continued seeking investments while his company was heavily in debt and facing serious cash-flow problems has now been sentenced to federal prison. More than 20 investors lost over $2.2 million after trusting his representations about the business and its projects.In a press release issued on October 28, 2026, the US Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California announced that Sanjeev Acharya, former president and CEO of SiliconSage Builders, had been sentenced to 18 months in prison for wire fraud and money laundering. US District Judge Charles R. Breyer also ordered him to pay $2,253,219.84 in restitution to victims and serve two years of supervised release. Acharya is scheduled to begin his prison sentence on January 9, 2027.How the real-estate investment business operatedAcharya, 58, of San Jose, was the president and CEO of SiliconSage Builders and several related companies. The business operated as a vertically integrated development and construction company, supporting investments in large residential and mixed-use real-estate projects across the San Francisco Bay Area. As part of his role, Acharya personally approached investors and encouraged them to put money into the company's property developments. The investment model depended on attracting funds to support construction and other real-estate activities.However, the company's financial position had deteriorated significantly by 2020. According to the plea agreement, the business was struggling partly because of the COVID-19 pandemic and had accumulated substantial debt. It was also experiencing serious cash-flow shortages and needed fresh investments to remain operational. Rather than disclosing these difficulties to potential investors, Acharya continued seeking money for the business.How investors were misledThe fraudulent scheme began in March 2020 and continued until October 26, 2020. During this period, Acharya solicited investments without informing people about the company's actual financial condition. According to the US Attorney's Office, he knew SiliconSage was in serious financial trouble but concealed its debt and cash-flow problems while persuading investors to provide additional funds.The investors were therefore not given important information that could have influenced their decisions about whether to invest. They were unaware that the company was struggling financially and required new money to survive. More than 20 investors were deceived during the scheme. Together, they suffered losses exceeding $2.2 million. The case highlights how financial difficulties within a property development business can affect people who invest their savings based on the expectation that their money will support viable projects.CEO pleaded guilty to wire fraud and a financial offenceAcharya was charged on September 5, 2025, in connection with the investment fraud. Rather than proceeding to trial, he pleaded guilty on January 6, 2026, to wire fraud and engaging in a monetary transaction involving property derived from fraud. Wire fraud is a federal offence involving the use of electronic communications or other forms of interstate communication to carry out a fraudulent scheme. The money laundering-related offence in his case concerned conducting a financial transaction with money obtained through unlawful activity.The investigation was conducted by the Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI), which examined the financial transactions and the movement of money connected with the scheme. US Attorney Craig H. Missakian said financial difficulties could never justify deceiving investors. He added that the prison sentence held Acharya accountable and demonstrated that people who exploit investors for financial gain could face serious consequences. John Abram, acting special agent in charge of the IRS-CI San Francisco Field Office, also highlighted the impact of financial fraud on individuals and families. He said the losses could put retirement plans, educational opportunities and financial security at risk.Court orders more than $2.25 million in restitutionUS District Judge Charles R. Breyer sentenced Acharya to 18 months in federal prison. In addition to the prison term, the judge imposed two years of supervised release and ordered him to pay $2,253,219.84 in restitution to the victims. Restitution is intended to compensate people who suffered financial losses because of a criminal offence. In this case, the amount ordered by the court reflects the financial harm caused to investors through the fraudulent scheme. Acharya is scheduled to report to prison on January 9, 2027.Assistant US Attorney Christiaan Highsmith prosecuted the case, with assistance from Janice Pagsanjan, Mimi Lam and Kevin Costello. The prosecution followed the investigation conducted by IRS-CI. The case serves as a reminder that property investment companies must be transparent about their financial condition when raising money. Even when a business is attempting to survive difficult market conditions, withholding important financial information from investors can carry serious criminal consequences.You use AI every day.
